newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia reaps mixed blessings from downtrodden yen.
newsitem.headline: Asia reaps mixed blessings from downtrodden yen.

text.p: Asian economies whose currencies are closely linked to the dollar are reaping mixed blessings from the yen's steep slide.
Several of Japan's Asian neighbours are suffering from a loss of export competitiveness due to their currencies' sharp jumps against the downtrodden yen.
But many of those same countries are also benefiting from cheaper Japanese imports, which spell lower production costs and could help trim their troublesome trade deficits.

Japan itself has reacted to the yen's 50 percent decline against the dollar since April 1995 with mixed feelings, welcoming a short-term boost for exports while worrying that the yen's sharp drop may later spark an equally steep rise.
Other Asian economies could be forgiven for harbouring similar ambivalence, if for different reasons.

On the export side of the equation, economists say a rise in the value of Asian currencies against the yen works to make their exports less competitive, both in Japan and in third markets where they face off against Japanese rivals.

"There is a loss of competitiveness, particularly for people like the (South) Koreans who are competing in third markets, and all the exporters are to some extent," said Alex Erskine, a regional economist for Citibank in Singapore.
Benefits to South Korean exporters from their currency's fall against the dollar risk being swamped by the yen's bigger decline against the greenback, officials and analysts say.

"The won has been depreciating against the dollar in line with the yen's decline. But the yen's fall has been much faster than the won's, and this will hurt South Korean exports," said a government official in Seoul.
In Hong Kong, where the currency is pegged at one U.S. dollar to 7.8 Hong Kong dollars, exports are also suffering.

"A rising dollar definitely affects our exports," said Joanne Yim, head of economic research at Hang Seng Bank in Hong Kong. But in a bid to keep their competitive edge, exporters shaved profit margins to keep export prices down, he added.
Taiwanese officials said the weak yen could hurt exports in the short term, but voiced little concern about the long term.
"The U.S. dollar will not always be strong, while the yen will not always be weak," one senior Taiwanese trade official said.
The yen's dive, however, has also brought the blessing of cheaper imports to many Asian nations, which depend heavily on Japanese components for their own exports.

"When looking at Singapore's export competitiveness, you really have to take into account the importance of imports in the production process," said Desmond Supple, a senior economist at research firm I.D.E.A. "While the Singapore dollar might be appreciating against many of its trading partners, they're still in a position where import costs are low and so underlying export competitiveness is strong."

Other Asian importers are also benefiting, with Malaysia in particular cheered by the yen's fall. Economists say Malaysia's trade deficit probably fell to about 2.0 billion ringgit ($805 million) in 1996 from 9.36 billion ringgit ($3.77 billion) in 1995 and further declines are in store.
Malaysia auto firms such as Proton Bhd are also getting an earnings boost from cheaper Japanese car parts.

"What you have seen in the past few months is a sharp reduction in the cost base for car manufacturers in Malaysia, and naturally that applies to a host of producers in Indonesia and Thailand," Daniel Lian, a regional economist at NatWest Markets in Singapore, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Countries such as Malaysia and the Philippines, with hefty chunks of foreign debt denominated in yen, are also applauding the yen's fall. "In a way, the country benefits when the yen depreciates because in terms of U.S. dollars our debt becomes lower," Philippine central bank Governor Gabriel Singson told RFTV last Friday.

Few in Asia, meanwhile, appear to be losing much sleep over the possibility that a weak yen could persuade Japanese firms, which have been shifting output offshore since the late 1980s, to rethink their investment strategies and move some output back home. Their moves overseas were prompted by a wish to cut costs in response to the yen's rise.
"The currency is just one of the factors, and the medium- to longer-term outlook is that the yen will still strengthen," said an economist with a large U.S. bank in Singapore.
He added: "The other factor is that Asia is still growing and offering great potential, so it makes sense for Japanese investors to tap into this economic growth."
